paper_id: Dong et al. - 2011 - SenSpire OS A Predictable, Flexible, and Efficient Operating System for Wireless Sensor Networks
title: SenSpire OS: A Predictable, Flexible, and Efficient Operating System for Wireless Sensor Networks
motivation: WSN nodes deployed in inaccessible areas operate unattended for long periods; existing OSs fail to bound interrupt latency or provide programming flexibility.
problem_framing: Three-way trade-off: interrupt latency predictability (bounded vs unbounded), programming flexibility (event-driven vs multithreaded), and resource efficiency.
key_insight: Two-phase interrupt servicing + priority ceiling protocol in kernel scheduler enables decoupling of event/thread subsystems while enabling stack sharing for memory efficiency.
method_signature: Native hybrid scheduling with differentiated kernel scheduler, two-phase interrupts, priority ceiling protocol, and stack sharing.
evaluation_criteria: Interrupt latency CDF, bottom half latency, scheduling overhead, program memory footprint, reprogramming file size.
negative_result_or_admitted_limitation: Two-phase interrupt servicing adds programming complexity: developers must reason about bottom halves vs top halves for synchronization.
evidence_for_taste: cannot prevent the applications from disabling interrupts
SenSpire OS achieves a more predictable interrupt latency
advances prior work by supporting programmer-assigned priority-based preemption
is able to employ stack sharing for optimizing resource utilization
CELF is 1.6-2.5 times larger than SELF
thinking_moves: Identify failure modes in prior work (atomic sections unbounded latency, tight coupling of subsystems)
Infer design requirements from observed problems
Derive joint solution: kernel-native hybrid scheduling enables both decoupling and stack sharing
Articulate that event preemption is necessary for predictability, not just thread preemption
Show how prelinking and chained references reduce module file size more than datatype compression
